article_title: C3-IoC: A Career Guidance System for Assessing Student Skills using Machine Learning and Network Visualisation
citation: Adán José-García, Alison Sneyd, Ana Melro, Anaïs Ollagnier, Georgina Tarling, Haiyang Zhang, Mark Stevenson, Richard Everson, Rudy Arthur. (2023). C3-IoC: A Career Guidance System for Assessing Student Skills using Machine Learning and Network Visualisation. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00317-y
title: C3-IoC career guidance system (three-module architecture)
description: C3-IoC is an online AI-based career guidance system helping undergraduates and high school students explore IT job roles. As the article states, "The system consists of three modules: (1) a novel knowledge base covering the full range of skills, both technical and non-technical...; (2) a user skill profiling module in which students' technical skills are collected using a CV parser and non-technical skills are self-assessed through a questionnaire; and (3) a job role matching and visualisation module". It supports self-evaluation of skills and exploration of emerging IT jobs via a personalised job network visualisation.
requirements: Users upload a PDF CV and complete a 24-question non-technical skills questionnaire, of which four questions are mandatory
A knowledge base of skills and job roles built from the IT job corpus and the O*NET general job corpus is required for matching
constraints: The article notes the accuracy of job role prediction is highly dependent on the information in the user profile, in particular the minimum number of questionnaire questions answered
The system primarily focuses on the IT sector, incorporating other job roles only at a coarse resolution
target_learning_goals: Career exploration in the IT sector
Self-evaluation and awareness of technical and non-technical skills
examples: Users progress through a three-stage journey: CV parser and questionnaire, radar-chart skill refinement, and a network map of the user's placement in the IT job role space

title: C3-IoC knowledge base built from the IT job corpus and the O*NET general job corpus
description: The C3-IoC knowledge base combines two complementary datasets. From the UK 'Find a job' website, crawled weekly from October 2018 to December 2019, "Duplicated jobs were removed, resulting in a corpus of 22,359 jobs"; text mining with a Word2Vec model extended a 100-skill seed list to 902 terms, manually cleaned to "an IT skill dictionary consisting of 195 unique skills", and 26 job roles were identified. From O*NET 2019 (version db_24), "we considered a total of 142 skills and 381 job roles", restricted to roles over 50% of respondents ranked as requiring a Bachelor's degree or higher.
requirements: Continuous curation from live labour market sources to keep up-to-date with emerging and changing roles
Manual cleaning and peer revision to merge synonyms and match non-technical skills between the two datasets
constraints: ESCO and O*NET lack up-to-date IT sector skills and roles, and ESCO does not consider discrete levels of importance of skills for specific job roles
The O*NET restriction to degree-level roles removed a large number of job roles, most described as 'physical' or 'manual'
Five IT job corpus non-technical skills could not be matched to O*NET questions and were excluded
target_learning_goals: Understanding which technical and non-technical skills are relevant for emerging IT jobs
examples: Each job role was represented as a weighted list of skills, where the weighting is the proportion of ads in that role containing that skill (Table 2 lists the 26 roles, e.g. software developer with 2374 jobs)

title: Job role network method: skill-level-aware similarity metric, RCA weighting, and Louvain community detection for projecting users into a job role space
description: The article proposes representing job roles and users as weighted skill vectors and matching them with a similarity metric in which "the distance between u and j does not increase if the user has at least the requisite skill level for the job role", so Sim(u,j) in [0,1] favours roles the user can meet. Job role networks are built with "the revealed comparative advantage index (RCA), which denotes the relative importance of a skill for a job role after accounting for skills which are common across many job roles" and a force-directed layout, with "the Louvain community detection algorithm" identifying job role types. This places students within communities of job roles, visualised for the IT job corpus and the general job corpus.
requirements: Skill importance ratings normalised in the range [0, 5] for both databases
A user skill profile with weighted technical and non-technical skills
constraints: The absence of an edge between nodes indicates job roles have no skills with effective needs in common
The general corpus was restricted to degree-level job roles, so the network shows only those roles
target_learning_goals: Understanding how one's skillset relates to communities of job roles
Exploring related career fields and the skills associated with specific occupations
examples: In the Bioinformatician example projection (Fig. 6), the top job role matches included Bioinformatic Scientist (96%) and Molecular and Cellular Biologist (91%), with the user located in the Science and Technology community
The general job corpus network has 11 communities and the IT job corpus network has 4 communities (Figs. 4 and 5)
